question_text: The work functions of Caesium (Cs), Potassium (K) and Sodium (Na) are 2.14 eV, 2.30 eV and 2.75 eV respectively. If incident electromagnetic radiation has an incident energy of 2.20 eV, which of these photosensitive surfaces may emit photoelectrons?

explanation.summary: Photoemission occurs only when the energy of the incident radiation is greater than the work function of the metal surface. By comparing the incident energy with the work functions of Cs, K, and Na, we can determine which metal will emit photoelectrons.

step_by_step.description: State the condition for the photoelectric effect. For photoelectrons to be emitted from a metal surface, the energy of the incident photon (E) must be greater than or equal to the work function (\(\phi\)) of the metal.

Identify the given values. The incident energy is \(E = 2.20 \text{ eV}\). The work functions are: \(\phi_{Cs} = 2.14 \text{ eV}\), \(\phi_{K} = 2.30 \text{ eV}\), and \(\phi_{Na} = 2.75 \text{ eV}\).
Compare the incident energy with the work function of each metal.
step_by_step.formula: For Caesium (Cs): \(2.20 \text{ eV} > 2.14 \text{ eV}\). The condition is met.\nFor Potassium (K): \(2.20 \text{ eV} < 2.30 \text{ eV}\). The condition is not met.\nFor Sodium (Na): \(2.20 \text{ eV} < 2.75 \text{ eV}\). The condition is not met.

step_by_step.description: Conclude which surface will emit photoelectrons. Since the incident energy is sufficient only for Caesium, only the Caesium surface may emit photoelectrons.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The incident energy of 2.20 eV is greater than the work function of Caesium (2.14 eV), so photoemission is possible from the Caesium surface. For both Potassium (2.30 eV) and Sodium (2.75 eV), the incident energy is less than their respective work functions, so no photoelectrons will be emitted from them.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: The work function of Potassium (K) is 2.30 eV, which is greater than the incident energy of 2.20 eV. Therefore, K will not emit photoelectrons.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: The work function of Sodium (Na) is 2.75 eV, which is significantly greater than the incident energy of 2.20 eV. Therefore, Na will not emit photoelectrons.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Since neither Na nor K will emit photoelectrons under these conditions, this option is incorrect.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the condition for photoemission (\(E > \phi\)).
Incorrectly comparing the energy values.
explanation.additional_notes: The work function is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a material. Any excess energy from the incident photon is converted into the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectron.

question_text: The ratio of frequencies of fundamental harmonic produced by an open pipe to that of a closed pipe having the same length is:

explanation.summary: This question asks for the ratio of the fundamental frequencies of an open organ pipe and a closed organ pipe of the same length. The ratio is found by using the standard formulas for the fundamental frequencies of both types of pipes.

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula for the fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe. An open pipe has antinodes at both ends. For the fundamental mode, the length of the pipe \(L\) is equal to half a wavelength (\(\lambda_o/2\)).
Calculate the fundamental frequency of the open pipe (\(f_o\)) using the wave speed \(v\).

Recall the formula for the fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe. A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. For the fundamental mode, the length of the pipe \(L\) is equal to one-quarter of a wavelength (\(\lambda_c/4\)).
Calculate the fundamental frequency of the closed pipe (\(f_c\)) using the wave speed \(v\).
Find the ratio of the frequency of the open pipe to the closed pipe.
The ratio is 2 : 1.

scientific_principles: Formation of Standing Waves in Air Columns
explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The fundamental frequency of an open pipe of length L is \(f_o = v/2L\). The fundamental frequency of a closed pipe of the same length L is \(f_c = v/4L\). The ratio \(f_o / f_c\) is \((v/2L) / (v/4L) = 2/1\).

incorrect_options_analysis.A: 1 : 3 is the ratio of the first harmonic to the third harmonic (first overtone) in a closed pipe.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: 3 : 1 is an incorrect ratio, possibly from inverting the ratio of first overtones.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: 1 : 2 is the inverse of the correct ratio, which would be the ratio of a closed pipe to an open pipe.

common_mistakes: Confusing the formulas for open and closed pipes.
Inverting the ratio (calculating closed:open instead of open:closed).
explanation.additional_notes: An open pipe can produce all harmonics (1, 2, 3, ...), while a closed pipe can only produce odd harmonics (1, 3, 5, ...).

question_text: The amount of energy required to form a soap bubble of radius 2 cm from a soap solution is nearly (surface tension of soap solution = \(0.03 \text{ N m}^{-1}\))

explanation.summary: The energy required to form a soap bubble is the product of the surface tension and the total increase in the surface area. A key point is that a soap bubble has two surfaces (inner and outer), which must be accounted for when calculating the total surface area.

step_by_step.description: Identify the formula for the energy required (Work Done) to create a surface area. The energy \(W\) is equal to the surface tension \(T\) multiplied by the change in surface area \(\Delta A\).
Recognize that a soap bubble has two surfaces: an inner surface and an outer surface. Therefore, the total surface area created is twice the surface area of a sphere of that radius.
Calculate the total surface area \(\Delta A\) of the soap bubble. The radius \(r = 2 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}\).
Substitute the value of the radius into the area formula.
Identify the given surface tension, \(T = 0.03 \text{ N m}^{-1}\).
Calculate the required energy \(W\) using the formula from Step 1.
Evaluate the final expression. Use \(\pi \approx 3.14\).
Compare the result with the given options. The calculated value is approximately \(3.01 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}\).

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The energy needed is calculated as \(W = T \times \Delta A\). For a soap bubble, there are two surfaces, so \(\Delta A = 2 \times 4\pi r^2\). Given \(T = 0.03 \text{ N/m}\) and \(r = 0.02 \text{ m}\), the energy is \(W = 0.03 \times 8\pi (0.02)^2 = 0.03 \times 8\pi \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 9.6\pi \times 10^{-5} \approx 30.14 \times 10^{-5} = 3.014 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.B: This value is significantly larger and may result from calculation errors.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: This value is ten times larger than the correct answer, possibly due to a mistake in handling powers of ten.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This value might be obtained if the factor of 2 for the two surfaces of the bubble is missed, and there are other calculation errors.

common_mistakes: Forgetting that a soap bubble has two surfaces and using \(\Delta A = 4\pi r^2\) instead of \(2 \times 4\pi r^2\).
Errors in unit conversion from cm to m.
Calculation mistakes with exponents.
explanation.additional_notes: For a liquid drop, there is only one surface, so the formula would be \(W = T \times (4\pi r^2)\).

question_text: A vehicle travels half the distance with speed \(v\) and the remaining distance with speed \(2v\). Its average speed is:

explanation.summary: The average speed is calculated as the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken. Since the vehicle covers two equal distances at different speeds, we calculate the time taken for each part and then use the average speed formula.

step_by_step.description: Define the formula for average speed.
Let the total distance be \(2d\). The vehicle travels the first half of the distance (\(d\)) with speed \(v\) and the second half (\(d\)) with speed \(2v\).
Calculate the time taken for the first half of the journey (\(t_1\)).
Calculate the time taken for the second half of the journey (\(t_2\)).
Calculate the total time taken (\(T\)).
Calculate the average speed using the total distance (\(2d\)) and total time (\(T\)).

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The average speed is the harmonic mean of the speeds when equal distances are covered. The formula is \(v_{avg} = \frac{2v_1v_2},{v_1+v_2}\). Substituting \(v_1 = v\) and \(v_2 = 2v\), we get \(v_{avg} = \frac{2(v)(2v)},{v+2v} = \frac{4v^2},{3v} = \frac{4v},{3}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.B: \(\frac{3},{4}v\) is the inverse of the correct answer.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: \(\frac{3},{2}v\) is the arithmetic mean of the speeds (\(\frac{v+2v},{2}\)), which is incorrect for averaging over distances.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: \(\frac{2},{3}v\) may result from an algebraic error in the calculation.

common_mistakes: Calculating the arithmetic mean of the speeds (\((v+2v)/2\)) instead of the correct average speed for equal distances.
Making errors in fraction algebra when calculating the total time.
explanation.additional_notes: When an object travels for equal time intervals at different speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\), the average speed is the arithmetic mean: \(v_{avg} = (v_1+v_2)/2\). When it travels equal distances at these speeds, the average speed is the harmonic mean: \(v_{avg} = 2v_1v_2 / (v_1+v_2)\).

question_text:
For Young’s double slit experiment, two statements are given below: 
Statement I : If the screen is moved away from the plane of slits, the angular separation of the fringes remains constant. 
Statement II : If the monochromatic source is replaced by another monochromatic source of larger wavelength, the angular separation of fringes decreases. 
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.A: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
options.B: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
options.C: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
options.D: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

explanation.summary: This question tests the understanding of the factors affecting fringe separation in Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE). We need to analyze how angular separation depends on the screen distance and the wavelength of light.

step_by_step.description: Analyze Statement I. Recall the formula for the angular separation (or angular fringe width) \(\theta\) in YDSE.

Observe the variables in the formula for angular separation. \(\theta\) depends on the wavelength of light \(\lambda\) and the distance between the slits \(d\). It does not depend on the distance between the slits and the screen, \(D\).

Conclude on Statement I. Since \(\theta\) is independent of \(D\), if the screen is moved away from the plane of slits (i.e., \(D\) is changed), the angular separation of the fringes remains constant. Therefore, Statement I is true.
Analyze Statement II. The statement says that if the monochromatic source is replaced by another with a larger wavelength (\(\lambda' > \lambda\)), the angular separation decreases.

Examine the relationship between angular separation \(\theta\) and wavelength \(\lambda\) from the formula \(\theta = \lambda/d\). Angular separation is directly proportional to the wavelength (\(\theta \propto \lambda\)).
Conclude on Statement II. If the wavelength \(\lambda\) increases, the angular separation \(\theta\) must also increase. The statement claims it decreases. Therefore, Statement II is false.
Combine the conclusions for both statements. Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Statement I is correct because angular separation \(\theta = \lambda/d\) is independent of the screen distance D. Statement II is incorrect because angular separation is directly proportional to wavelength (\(\theta \propto \lambda\)); thus, increasing the wavelength would increase, not decrease, the angular separation.

incorrect_options_analysis.B: This is incorrect because Statement I is true and Statement II is false.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: This is incorrect because Statement II is false.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This is incorrect because Statement I is true.

common_mistakes: Confusing angular separation (\(\theta = \lambda/d\)) with linear fringe width (\(\beta = \lambda D/d\)). The linear fringe width *does* increase as the screen is moved away.
explanation.additional_notes: While angular separation remains constant when D changes, the linear distance between fringes on the screen (fringe width, \(\beta\)) increases because \(\beta = D\theta\). This is an important distinction to remember.

question_text: Light travels a distance \(x\) in time \(t_1\) in air and \(10x\) in time \(t_2\) in another denser medium. What is the critical angle for this medium?

explanation.summary: This problem requires calculating the critical angle for a medium based on the travel times of light over different distances in air and the medium. The solution involves finding the speeds of light in both media, calculating the refractive index, and then using the formula for the critical angle.
key_concepts: Speed of Light in a Medium

step_by_step.description: Calculate the speed of light in air (\(v_{air}\)).
Calculate the speed of light in the denser medium (\(v_{med}\)).
Calculate the refractive index (\(\mu\)) of the denser medium with respect to air. The refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed of light in the medium.
Recall the formula for the critical angle (\(C\)). The sine of the critical angle is the reciprocal of the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer medium (air).
Substitute the expression for the refractive index \(\mu\) into the critical angle formula.
Solve for the critical angle \(C\).

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The speed in air is \(v_a = x/t_1\) and in the medium is \(v_m = 10x/t_2\). The refractive index is \(\mu = v_a/v_m = (x/t_1) / (10x/t_2) = t_2/(10t_1)\). The critical angle \(C\) is given by \(\sin(C) = 1/\mu = 10t_1/t_2\). Therefore, \(C = \sin^{-1}(10t_1/t_2)\).

incorrect_options_analysis.A: This option is the inverse of the correct expression inside the arcsin.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: This option incorrectly omits the factor of 10.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This option represents \(\sin^{-1}(\mu)\), not \(\sin^{-1}(1/\mu)\).

common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio when calculating the refractive index (i.e., calculating \(v_{med}/v_{air}\)).
Confusing the formula for critical angle, using \(\sin(C) = \mu\) instead of \(\sin(C) = 1/\mu\).
explanation.additional_notes: For total internal reflection to occur, light must travel from a denser medium to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle.

question_text: An AC source is connected to a capacitor C. Due to a decrease in its operating frequency:

explanation.summary: This question explores the relationship between frequency, capacitive reactance, and current in a purely capacitive AC circuit. A decrease in frequency leads to an increase in capacitive reactance, which in turn causes a decrease in the current flowing through the capacitor.

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula for capacitive reactance (\(X_C\)). It is inversely proportional to the angular frequency (\(\omega\)) and capacitance (\(C\)).

Analyze the effect of a decrease in operating frequency (\(f\)) on capacitive reactance (\(X_C\)). Since \(X_C\) is inversely proportional to \(f\), a decrease in \(f\) will cause an increase in \(X_C\).
Recall Ohm's law for AC circuits. The current (\(I\)) through the capacitor is given by the voltage (\(V\)) divided by the reactance (\(X_C\)).
Analyze the effect of the change in \(X_C\) on the current (\(I\)). Since \(X_C\) increases (from Step 2) and the current \(I\) is inversely proportional to \(X_C\), the current \(I\) will decrease.

Relate the conduction current to the displacement current in a capacitor. For an ideal capacitor, the displacement current (\(I_d\)) is equal to the conduction current (\(I\)) flowing in the wires connected to it.
Conclude the effect on the displacement current. Since the conduction current \(I\) decreases, the displacement current \(I_d\) also decreases.

scientific_principles: Maxwell's Equations (specifically the concept of displacement current)
explanation.correct_option_reasoning: When the frequency \(f\) of the AC source decreases, the capacitive reactance \(X_C = 1/(2\pi f C)\) increases. The current in the circuit is \(I = V/X_C\). As \(X_C\) increases, the current \(I\) decreases. In a capacitor, the displacement current is equal to the conduction current. Therefore, the displacement current decreases.

incorrect_options_analysis.B: Capacitive reactance is dependent on frequency (\(X_C \propto 1/f\)), so it cannot remain constant when the frequency changes.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Capacitive reactance increases when frequency decreases, it does not decrease.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Since the current is inversely proportional to the reactance, and the reactance increases, the displacement current must decrease, not increase.

common_mistakes: Confusing the relationship for capacitive reactance (\(X_C \propto 1/f\)) with that for inductive reactance (\(X_L \propto f\)).
explanation.additional_notes: Displacement current was introduced by Maxwell to make the laws of electromagnetism consistent. It is associated with a changing electric field and is crucial for the existence of electromagnetic waves.

question_text: In a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in free space, the electric field component oscillates sinusoidally at a frequency of \(2.0 \times 10^{10} \text{ Hz}\) and amplitude \(48 \text{ V m}^{-1}\). Then the amplitude of the oscillating magnetic field is (Speed of light in free space = \(3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}\))

explanation.summary: This question requires finding the amplitude of the magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave, given the amplitude of the electric field. The relationship between the amplitudes of the electric and magnetic fields in an EM wave in free space is a fundamental concept.

step_by_step.description: Recall the relationship between the amplitudes of the electric field (\(E_0\)) and the magnetic field (\(B_0\)) in an electromagnetic wave travelling in a vacuum (free space).

Identify the given values from the question. Amplitude of the electric field, \(E_0 = 48 \text{ V m}^{-1}\). Speed of light in free space, \(c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}\). The frequency is extra information not needed for this calculation.
Rearrange the formula to solve for the amplitude of the magnetic field, \(B_0\).
Substitute the given values into the formula and calculate \(B_0\).
Express the answer in standard scientific notation.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The ratio of the amplitudes of the electric field (E₀) and magnetic field (B₀) in an electromagnetic wave is equal to the speed of light (c). Using the formula \(B_0 = E_0 / c\), with \(E_0 = 48 \text{ V/m}\) and \(c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\), we get \(B_0 = 48 / (3 \times 10^8) = 16 \times 10^{-8} \text{ T} = 1.6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.B: Incorrect by a factor of 10.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Incorrect by a factor of 100.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This value (\(16 \times 10^{-8} \text{ T}\)) is correct before converting to standard scientific notation.

common_mistakes: Using the formula incorrectly, for example, \(B_0 = E_0 \times c\).
Making errors with powers of ten during the calculation.
explanation.additional_notes: In an EM wave, the electric field, magnetic field, and the direction of propagation are all mutually perpendicular. The frequency of oscillation is the same for both the electric and magnetic fields.

question_text: A football player is moving southward and suddenly turns eastward with the same speed to avoid an opponent. The force that acts on the player while turning is:

explanation.summary: To find the direction of the force, we must first find the direction of the acceleration. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. By finding the change in the velocity vector, we can determine the direction of the force acting on the player.

step_by_step.description: Define a coordinate system. Let the positive y-axis be North (\(+\hat{j}\)) and the positive x-axis be East (\(+\hat{i}\)). Therefore, South is \(-\hat{j}\) and West is \(-\hat{i}\).
Write the initial velocity vector (\(\vec{v}_i\)). The player is moving southward with speed \(v\).
Write the final velocity vector (\(\vec{v}_f\)). The player turns eastward with the same speed \(v\).
Calculate the change in velocity vector (\(\Delta\vec{v}\)).

Determine the direction of the change in velocity vector. The vector \(v \hat{i} + v \hat{j}\) has a positive x-component (East) and a positive y-component (North). Therefore, the direction of \(\Delta\vec{v}\) is North-East.

Relate the direction of force to the direction of acceleration using Newton's Second Law. The force \(\vec{F}\) is in the same direction as the acceleration \(\vec{a}\), which is in the same direction as the change in velocity \(\Delta\vec{v}\).
Conclude the direction of the force. Since the force is in the same direction as \(\Delta\vec{v}\), the force acts along the North-East direction.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The initial velocity is \(\vec{v}_i = -v\hat{j}\) (South). The final velocity is \(\vec{v}_f = v\hat{i}\) (East). The change in velocity is \(\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = v\hat{i} - (-v\hat{j}) = v\hat{i} + v\hat{j}\). This resultant vector points towards the North-East. According to Newton's second law (\(\vec{F} = m\vec{a}\)), the force is in the direction of the acceleration, which is the direction of the change in velocity. Thus, the force is along the North-East.

incorrect_options_analysis.B: South-West (\(-\hat{i} - \hat{j}\)) would be the direction if the player went from North to West.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Along eastward is the direction of the final velocity, not the change in velocity.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Along northward would imply only the y-component of velocity changed, which is not the case.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly performing vector subtraction, for example, adding the vectors instead of subtracting the initial from the final.
Confusing the direction of velocity with the direction of change in velocity (acceleration).
explanation.additional_notes: The force required to change the direction of motion is a centripetal force. In this case, it's provided by the friction between the player's shoes and the ground.

question_text: The temperature of a gas is \(-50^{\circ}\text{C}\). To what temperature the gas should be heated so that the rms speed is increased by 3 times?

explanation.summary: This problem relates the rms speed of gas molecules to the absolute temperature. The key is to convert the initial temperature to Kelvin, determine the final rms speed based on the given increase, and then calculate the required final temperature in Kelvin, converting it back to Celsius if needed.

step_by_step.description: Convert the initial temperature from Celsius to Kelvin. The absolute temperature \(T\) in Kelvin is \(T(K) = T(^{\circ}C) + 273\).
Interpret the phrase 'increased by 3 times'. If the initial speed is \(v_1\), an increase *of* 3 times would be \(3v_1\), making the final speed \(v_2 = v_1 + 3v_1 = 4v_1\).
Recall the relationship between rms speed (\(v_{rms}\)) and absolute temperature (\(T\)). The rms speed is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature.
Set up a ratio to find the final temperature \(T_2\).
Substitute the values from steps 1 and 2 into the ratio.
Solve for \(T_2\) by squaring both sides.
Convert the final temperature \(T_2\) back to Celsius to check the options.
Compare the result with the given options. The calculated value \(3295^{\circ}\text{C}\) matches option D.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: First, convert the initial temperature to Kelvin: \(T_1 = -50 + 273 = 223 \text{ K}\). 'Increased by 3 times' means the final speed \(v_2\) is \(v_1 + 3v_1 = 4v_1\). Since \(v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}\), we have \(v_2/v_1 = \sqrt{T_2/T_1}\). This gives \(4 = \sqrt{T_2/223}\). Squaring both sides gives \(16 = T_2/223\), so \(T_2 = 16 \times 223 = 3568 \text{ K}\). Converting back to Celsius: \(3568 - 273 = 3295^{\circ}\text{C}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.A: 3097 K is an incorrect value, possibly from calculation errors.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: 223 K is the initial temperature in Kelvin, not the final temperature.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: This might result from misinterpreting 'increased by 3 times' as \(v_2 = 3v_1\), which would lead to \(T_2 = 9T_1 = 9 \times 223 = 2007 \text{ K} = 1734^{\circ}\text{C}\), which is also not this option.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert temperatures to Kelvin before using the formula.
Misinterpreting the phrase 'increased by 3 times'. It can be ambiguous, but in this context, it implies the final value is 4 times the initial value.
Errors in the final conversion back to Celsius.
explanation.additional_notes: The wording 'increased to 3 times' would mean \(v_2 = 3v_1\). The wording 'increased by 3 times' means \(v_2 = v_1 + 3v_1 = 4v_1\). This ambiguity in language is a common trap in physics problems.

question_text: Resistance of a carbon resistor determined from colour codes is \((22000 \pm 5\%) \Omega\). The colour of the third band must be:

explanation.summary: This question requires knowledge of the standard color code for carbon resistors. The resistance value is given, and we need to identify the color of the third band, which represents the multiplier.

step_by_step.description: Understand the structure of a 4-band resistor color code. The first two bands represent the first two significant digits of the resistance value, the third band is the multiplier, and the fourth band is the tolerance.
Express the given resistance value in scientific notation to easily identify the significant figures and the multiplier.

Identify the components from the rewritten resistance value: 
- First significant digit: 2 
- Second significant digit: 2 
- Multiplier: \(10^3\)
Recall the color code mnemonic (e.g., 'BB ROY of Great Britain has a Very Good Wife'). The third band corresponds to the power of 10 multiplier.

Find the color corresponding to the multiplier \(10^3\).
- Black: \(10^0\)
- Brown: \(10^1\)
- Red: \(10^2\)
- Orange: \(10^3\)
- Yellow: \(10^4\)
... and so on.
The multiplier is \(10^3\), which corresponds to the color Orange. Therefore, the third band must be Orange.

scientific_principles: Standard EIA Color Code for Resistors
explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The resistance is given as \(22000 \Omega\), which can be written as \(22 \times 10^3 \Omega\). In the resistor color code, the first band represents the first digit (2 = Red), the second band represents the second digit (2 = Red), and the third band represents the multiplier. The multiplier here is \(10^3\), which corresponds to the color Orange.

incorrect_options_analysis.B: Yellow corresponds to a multiplier of \(10^4\), which would give a resistance of \(220000 \Omega\).
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Red corresponds to a multiplier of \(10^2\), which would give a resistance of \(2200 \Omega\). Red is the color for the first two bands (digit 2).
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Green corresponds to a multiplier of \(10^5\), which would give a resistance of \(2200000 \Omega\).

common_mistakes: Confusing the digit color with the multiplier color.
Being off by one in the color code sequence.
Looking at the tolerance band (5% = Gold) instead of the multiplier band.
explanation.additional_notes: The full color code for this resistor would be Red (2), Red (2), Orange (\(10^3\)), and Gold (±5%).

question_text: A bullet is fired from a gun at the speed of \(280 \text{ m s}^{-1}\) in the direction \(30^{\circ}\) above the horizontal. The maximum height attained by the bullet is (\(g = 9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}\), \(\sin30^{\circ} = 0.5\))

explanation.summary: This is a classic projectile motion problem that requires calculating the maximum height reached by an object launched at an angle. The solution involves using the standard formula for maximum height in projectile motion.

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula for the maximum height (H) attained by a projectile.

Identify the given values: 
- Initial speed, \(u = 280 	ext{ m s}^{-1}\) 
- Angle of projection, \(	heta = 30^{\circ}\) 
- Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 9.8 	ext{ m s}^{-2}\) 
- \(\sin30^{\circ} = 0.5\)
Substitute these values into the maximum height formula.
Calculate the numerical value.
Simplify the expression.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Using the formula for maximum height of a projectile, \(H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta},{2g}\). We are given \(u=280\), \(\theta=30^{\circ}\), and \(g=9.8\). The vertical component of initial velocity is \(u_y = u \sin \theta = 280 \times 0.5 = 140 \text{ m/s}\). At maximum height, final vertical velocity is 0. Using \(v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gH\), we get \(0 = (140)^2 - 2(9.8)H\). So, \(H = \frac{140^2},{2 \times 9.8} = \frac{19600},{19.6} = 1000 \text{ m}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.B: Incorrect value, likely due to a calculation error.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Incorrect value, possibly from using \(\sin\theta\) instead of \(\sin^2\theta\) or other miscalculation.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Incorrect value, possibly from a mistake in the formula, such as forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to square the \(\sin \theta\) term.
Using the cosine of the angle instead of the sine.
Simple arithmetic errors during calculation.

question_text: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 50% when its source is at a temperature of \(327^{\circ}\text{C}\). The temperature of the sink is:

Convert the given source temperature from Celsius to Kelvin.
Convert the given efficiency from a percentage to a decimal.
Substitute the known values into the efficiency formula.
Solve the equation for \(T_{sink}\) in Kelvin.
Convert the sink temperature back from Kelvin to Celsius to match the options.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is \(\eta = 1 - T_{sink}/T_{source}\), where temperatures are in Kelvin. Given \(\eta = 0.5\) and \(T_{source} = 327 + 273 = 600 \text{ K}\). Substituting these values, \(0.5 = 1 - T_{sink}/600\). This gives \(T_{sink}/600 = 0.5\), so \(T_{sink} = 300 \text{ K}\). question_text: In a series LCR circuit, the inductance L is \(10 \text{ mH}\), capacitance C is \(1 \mu\text{F}\) and resistance R is \(100 \Omega\). The frequency at which resonance occurs is:

explanation.summary: This problem requires calculating the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit. The resonant frequency depends only on the inductance (L) and capacitance (C) and can be found using the standard formula. The resistance (R) affects the sharpness of the resonance but not the frequency itself.

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula for the resonant angular frequency (\(\omega_0\)) and the resonant frequency (\(f_0\)) of a series LCR circuit.
Identify and convert the given values of L and C to SI units.\n- Inductance, \(L = 10 \text{ mH} = 10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ H}\)\n- Capacitance, \(C = 1 \mu\text{F} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}\)
Calculate the product LC.
Calculate the resonant angular frequency \(\omega_0\).
Calculate the resonant frequency \(f_0\) in Hz.
Convert the frequency to kHz and compare with the options.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The resonance frequency \(f_0\) is given by the formula \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). Given \(L = 10 \text{ mH} = 10^{-2} \text{ H}\) and \(C = 1 \mu\text{F} = 10^{-6} \text{ F}\). Then, \(LC = 10^{-8} \text{ s}^2\) and \(\sqrt{LC} = 10^{-4} \text{ s}\). So, \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi \times 10^{-4}) = 10^4 / (2\pi) \approx 1592 \text{ Hz} = 1.592 \text{ kHz}\).

incorrect_options_analysis.A: This is the approximate value of \(1/(2\pi)\), missing the \(10^4\) factor. Or it could be a miscalculation of angular frequency.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Incorrect value, likely due to a calculation error.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This value is 10 times the correct frequency.

Confusing angular frequency (\(\omega\), in rad/s) with frequency (\(f\), in Hz).
Forgetting the \(2\pi\) factor in the frequency formula.
explanation.additional_notes: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the inductive reactance (\(X_L\)) equals the capacitive reactance (\(X_C\)). This results in the minimum impedance (equal to R) and maximum current for a given voltage.

question_text: If \(\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = 0\) over a surface, then:

options.A: All the charges must necessarily be inside the surface
options.B: The electric field inside the surface is necessarily uniform
options.C: The number of flux lines entering the surface must be equal to the number of flux lines leaving it
options.D: The magnitude of the electric field on the surface is constant

explanation.summary: This question tests the understanding of Gauss's Law for electrostatics. The integral \(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S}\) represents the total electric flux through a closed surface S. Understanding the implications of this flux being zero is key.

step_by_step.description: Identify the given expression. The expression \(\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S}\) represents the total electric flux (\(\Phi_E\)) passing through the closed surface S.
State Gauss's Law, which relates the total electric flux through a closed surface to the net charge enclosed by that surface (\(q_{enc}\)).
Apply the given condition \(\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = 0\). According to Gauss's Law, this implies that the net enclosed charge \(q_{enc}\) is zero.

Interpret the physical meaning of zero net flux. Electric flux is a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through a surface. A positive flux corresponds to lines leaving the surface, and a negative flux corresponds to lines entering. Zero net flux means that the number of field lines entering the surface is exactly equal to the number of field lines leaving it.

Evaluate the given options based on this understanding:
- A: Incorrect. The net charge inside is zero, which could mean there are no charges inside, or there are charges that sum to zero (like an electric dipole). Also, there could be charges outside the surface.
- B: Incorrect. The electric field inside is not necessarily zero or uniform. For example, a dipole inside the surface would create a non-uniform field, but the net flux would be zero. An external charge would also create a non-uniform field inside.
- C: Correct. This is the definition of zero net electric flux.
- D: Incorrect. The electric field magnitude on the surface is not necessarily constant. Consider an external point charge near the surface; the field would be stronger on the side closer to the charge.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The integral \(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S}\) represents the net electric flux through a closed surface. According to Gauss's law, this flux is proportional to the net charge enclosed. If the net flux is zero, it means the net charge enclosed is zero. Visually, this implies that every electric field line that enters the closed surface must also leave it. Therefore, the number of flux lines entering equals the number of flux lines leaving.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: The net charge inside is zero, but this does not mean there are no charges. An electric dipole could be inside, for instance.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: The electric field inside is not necessarily zero or uniform. An external charge can create a non-zero, non-uniform field inside the surface even if the net flux is zero.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: The electric field magnitude can vary over the surface. The condition is about the net flux (the integral of \(\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S}\)), not the magnitude of \(\vec{E}\) itself.

common_mistakes: Confusing zero flux with zero electric field. A non-zero electric field can exist everywhere on and inside the surface even if the net flux is zero.
Assuming zero enclosed charge means no charges are inside the surface, rather than the sum of charges being zero.

question_text: Two bodies of mass \(m\) and \(9m\) are placed at a distance \(R\). The gravitational potential on the line joining the bodies where the gravitational field equals zero, will be (G = gravitational constant):

explanation.summary: This problem is a two-step process. First, we must find the location between the two masses where the net gravitational field is zero. This point is known as a neutral point. Second, we calculate the total gravitational potential at this specific location due to both masses.

step_by_step.description: Find the point where the gravitational field is zero. Let this point be at a distance \(x\) from the mass \(m\) and \(R-x\) from the mass \(9m\). The gravitational fields from the two masses must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction at this point.
Solve for \(x\). Cancel \(Gm\) from both sides and take the square root.
Cross-multiply and solve for \(x\) in terms of \(R\).
Determine the distances of the zero-field point from both masses. The distance from \(m\) is \(x = R/4\). The distance from \(9m\) is \(R-x = R - R/4 = 3R/4\).
Calculate the total gravitational potential (\(V\)) at this point. Gravitational potential is a scalar quantity, so we add the potentials due to each mass.
Substitute the distances found in step 4 into the potential formula.
Simplify the expression to find the final potential.

scientific_principles: Principle of Superposition for Fields and Potentials
explanation.correct_option_reasoning: First, find the point of zero gravitational field at distance x from mass m. \(Gm/x^2 = G(9m)/(R-x)^2\), which gives \(x = R/4\). The distance from 9m is \(R-x = 3R/4\). Now, calculate the potential at this point: \(V = -Gm/x - G(9m)/(R-x)\). Substituting the distances: \(V = -Gm/(R/4) - 9Gm/(3R/4) = -4Gm/R - 12Gm/R = -16Gm/R\).

incorrect_options_analysis.B: Incorrect numerical value, likely from a calculation error.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Incorrect numerical value, possibly from an error in finding the location of the neutral point.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: This is only one component of the total potential (the potential due to the 9m mass at that point).

common_mistakes: Making an error while solving for the position \(x\).
Confusing the vector nature of fields (which cancel) with the scalar nature of potential (which adds up, with its negative sign).
Calculation errors when summing the potentials.

explanation.summary: To find the current in the circuit, we apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to the single loop. We sum the electromotive forces (EMFs) of the batteries and the voltage drops across the resistors to find the net current and its direction.

step_by_step.description: Assume a direction for the current flow. Let's assume the current \(I\) flows clockwise, from A to B through the external resistor E.
Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to the loop, starting from point A and moving clockwise. The sum of all potential changes in a closed loop is zero.

Write down the KVL equation based on the assumed circuit diagram. The 10V battery supports the clockwise current (potential gain), while the 5V battery opposes it (potential drop). All resistors cause a potential drop.
Simplify the equation by combining the EMFs and resistances.
Solve for the current \(I\).

Determine the direction of the current. Since the calculated value of \(I\) is positive, our initial assumption of a clockwise direction was correct. Therefore, the current flows from A to B through the external resistor E.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Applying KVL to the loop, the net EMF is \(10V - 5V = 5V\) (since the batteries oppose each other). The total resistance in the series circuit is \(R_{total} = 2\Omega + 1\Omega + 7\Omega = 10\Omega\). Using Ohm's Law for the entire circuit, the current is \(I = \text{Net EMF} / R_{total} = 5V / 10\Omega = 0.5 \text{ A}\). question_text: The angular acceleration of a body, moving along the circumference of a circle, is:

options.A: Along the tangent to its position
options.C: Along the radius, away from centre
options.D: Along the radius towards the centre

explanation.summary: This question tests the understanding of the vector nature of rotational quantities. Angular velocity and angular acceleration are axial vectors, meaning their direction is along the axis of rotation.

step_by_step.description: Recall the definitions of linear and angular quantities in circular motion. Linear velocity (tangential velocity) is along the tangent. Linear acceleration has two components: centripetal (radial) and tangential.
Recall the definition of angular acceleration (\(\vec{\alpha}\)). It is the rate of change of angular velocity (\(\vec{\omega}\)).

Identify the nature of angular velocity (\(\vec{\omega}\)) and angular acceleration (\(\vec{\alpha}\)). They are both axial vectors. The direction of an axial vector for rotation is defined to be along the axis of rotation.

Determine the specific direction using the Right-Hand Rule. If you curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation, your thumb points in the direction of the angular velocity vector \(\vec{\omega}\). The angular acceleration \(\vec{\alpha}\) is in the same direction as \(\vec{\omega}\) if the body is speeding up, and in the opposite direction if it is slowing down, but it is always collinear with the axis of rotation.

Evaluate the options:
- A: This is the direction of tangential velocity.
- B: This is the correct direction for any axial vector in rotation.
- C: This is the direction of centrifugal force (in a rotating frame).
- D: This is the direction of centripetal acceleration.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Angular velocity (\(\vec{\omega}\)) and angular acceleration (\(\vec{\alpha}\)) are defined as axial vectors. Their direction is perpendicular to the plane of rotation and lies along the axis of rotation, as determined by the right-hand rule. The other options describe linear quantities: tangential velocity (tangent) and centripetal acceleration (radius towards the center).

incorrect_options_analysis.A: The tangential direction corresponds to the linear velocity vector.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: The direction along the radius away from the center has no standard physical quantity associated with it in inertial frames.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: The direction along the radius towards the center corresponds to the centripetal acceleration vector.

question_text: The half-life of a radioactive substance is 20 minutes. In how much time, the activity of the substance drops to \(\left(\frac{1},{16}\right)^{\text{th}}\) of its initial value?

explanation.summary: This problem involves the concept of radioactive decay and half-life. We need to determine how many half-lives are required for the activity to reduce to 1/16th of its initial value and then calculate the total time elapsed.

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula relating the activity \(A\) at time \(t\) to the initial activity \(A_0\) and the number of half-lives \(n\).
Use the given information that the activity drops to \(1/16\) of its initial value.
Set the two expressions equal to each other to solve for the number of half-lives, \(n\).
Recognize that \(16 = 2^4\).
From the equation, determine the value of \(n\).
Calculate the total time elapsed. The total time is the number of half-lives multiplied by the duration of one half-life (\(T_{1/2}\)).
Substitute the values \(n=4\) and \(T_{1/2} = 20\) minutes.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The activity \(A\) after \(n\) half-lives is given by \(A = A_0(1/2)^n\). We are given \(A/A_0 = 1/16\). So, \((1/2)^n = 1/16 = (1/2)^4\), which means \(n = 4\) half-lives have passed. Since one half-life is 20 minutes, the total time is \(4 \times 20 = 80\) minutes.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: 60 minutes corresponds to 3 half-lives, where the activity would be \(1/8\) of the initial value.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: 20 minutes is one half-life, where the activity would be \(1/2\) of the initial value.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: 40 minutes corresponds to 2 half-lives, where the activity would be \(1/4\) of the initial value.

common_mistakes: Miscalculating the power of 2 (e.g., thinking \(2^3=16\)).
Confusing the number of half-lives with the total time.
explanation.additional_notes: The activity of a radioactive sample follows the same exponential decay law as the number of undecayed nuclei.

question_text: The venturi-meter works on:

question_text: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is:

explanation.summary: This question tests a fundamental law of magnetism, often referred to as Gauss's law for magnetism. It describes a key property of magnetic fields.

step_by_step.description: Recall the definition of magnetic flux. It is a measure of the total magnetic field lines passing through a given surface.
State Gauss's law for magnetism. This is one of the four Maxwell's equations. It states that the net magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero.

Understand the physical implication of this law. Magnetic field lines always form closed loops; they do not start or end at a point. This means that for any closed surface, the number of magnetic field lines entering the surface is always equal to the number of lines leaving it.

Relate this to the non-existence of magnetic monopoles. If magnetic monopoles (isolated north or south poles) existed, they would be sources or sinks of magnetic field lines, and the flux through a surface enclosing a monopole would be non-zero. Since monopoles have never been observed, the net flux is always zero.
Conclude that the net magnetic flux through any closed surface must be zero.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: According to Gauss's law for magnetism, the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero. This is a consequence of the fact that magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops and there are no magnetic monopoles (isolated north or south poles) to act as sources or sinks of the field lines. Therefore, for any closed surface, the magnetic flux entering it equals the magnetic flux leaving it.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: Infinity is not a physically meaningful value for flux in this context.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: A negative net flux would imply that a net 'south' pole is enclosed within the surface, which is not possible.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: A positive net flux would imply that a net 'north' pole is enclosed within the surface, which is not possible.

common_mistakes: Confusing Gauss's law for magnetism with Gauss's law for electricity. The net electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge and is not always zero.

question_text:
Given below are two statements: 
Statement I: Photovoltaic devices can convert optical radiation into electricity. 
Statement II: Zener diode is designed to operate under reverse bias in the breakdown region. 
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.

options.A: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
options.B: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
options.C: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
options.D: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

explanation.summary: This question assesses knowledge of two different semiconductor devices: photovoltaic devices (like solar cells) and Zener diodes. We need to evaluate the correctness of the statements describing their primary function and operating principle.

step_by_step.description: Analyze Statement I. It claims that photovoltaic devices convert optical radiation (light) into electricity. This phenomenon is known as the photovoltaic effect.

Recall the function of devices like solar cells. They are p-n junctions that, when illuminated, generate a potential difference (voltage) due to the creation of electron-hole pairs by photons. This directly converts light energy into electrical energy. Thus, Statement I is correct.
Analyze Statement II. It describes the operating principle of a Zener diode. It states the diode is designed for operation under reverse bias in the breakdown region.

Recall the characteristics of a Zener diode. It is a specially doped p-n junction that has a sharp, well-defined breakdown voltage when reverse biased. In this breakdown region, the voltage across the diode remains nearly constant even if the current changes significantly. This property is used for voltage regulation. Thus, Statement II is correct.
Combine the analysis of both statements. Since both Statement I and Statement II are correct descriptions of their respective devices, the correct option is that both are correct.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Statement I is correct. Photovoltaic devices, such as solar cells, are fundamentally designed to convert light energy (optical radiation) into electrical energy. Statement II is also correct. A Zener diode is specifically engineered to operate in the reverse breakdown region, where it maintains a stable voltage, making it useful as a voltage regulator. Since both statements are factually correct, this option is the right choice.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: Incorrect, as Statement II is also correct.
incorrect_options_analysis.B: Incorrect, as Statement I is also correct.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Incorrect, as both statements are correct.

question_text: The errors in the measurement which arise due to unpredictable fluctuations in temperature and voltage supply are:

explanation.summary: This question asks to classify a specific type of measurement error. Errors caused by unpredictable and uncontrollable fluctuations in experimental conditions are defined as random errors.

step_by_step.description: Analyze the source of the error described: 'unpredictable fluctuations in temperature and voltage supply'. The key word here is 'unpredictable'.

Define the different types of errors listed in the options:
- **Random errors:** Errors that occur irregularly and are random in magnitude and direction. They are caused by unpredictable fluctuations in experimental conditions.
- **Systematic errors:** Errors that tend to be in one direction, either positive or negative. They are often due to a problem with the instrument (instrumental error) or the experimental procedure.
- **Least count errors:** A type of random error associated with the resolution of the measuring instrument.
- **Instrumental errors:** A type of systematic error arising from imperfect design, calibration, or zero error in the instrument.
- **Personal errors:** Errors arising from an individual's bias, lack of proper setting of the apparatus, or carelessness in taking observations.
Match the description in the question to the definitions. The unpredictable fluctuations in external conditions like temperature and voltage directly fit the definition of random errors.

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: Random errors are those that occur due to unpredictable and uncontrollable variations in experimental conditions, such as fluctuations in temperature, voltage, or mechanical vibrations. These errors cause the measured value to be sometimes higher and sometimes lower than the true value. The description in the question perfectly matches the definition of random errors.

incorrect_options_analysis.A: Least count error is the error associated with the smallest division on the measurement scale, not fluctuations in external conditions.
incorrect_options_analysis.C: Instrumental errors are a type of systematic error due to a faulty instrument, like an incorrect calibration. They are predictable if the fault is known.
incorrect_options_analysis.D: Personal errors are due to the observer, such as parallax error or reaction time, and are not caused by external environmental fluctuations.

common_mistakes: Confusing random errors with systematic errors. Systematic errors are consistent and repeatable, while random errors are unpredictable.
explanation.additional_notes: Random errors can be minimized by taking multiple measurements and calculating the average, as the random positive and negative deviations tend to cancel out.

question_text: The x-t graph of a particle performing simple harmonic motion is shown in the figure. The acceleration of the particle at \(t = 2 \text{ s}\) is:

Determine the time period (T) of the oscillation. The particle completes one-quarter of a cycle in 2 seconds (from mean to extreme position). Therefore, the full time period is \(T = 4 \times 2 = 8 \text{ s}\).

Determine the position of the particle at \(t = 2 \text{ s}\). According to the graph, at \(t=2\text{ s}\), the particle is at its maximum positive displacement, so \(x = +A = +1 \text{ m}\).

question_text: The radius of the inner most orbit of a hydrogen atom is \(5.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}\). What is the radius of the third allowed orbit of the hydrogen atom?

explanation.summary: This question applies the Bohr model for the hydrogen atom to find the radius of a specific electron orbit. The radius of the nth orbit is directly proportional to the square of the principal quantum number (n).

step_by_step.description: Recall the formula for the radius of the nth allowed orbit (\(r_n\)) in the Bohr model of a hydrogen atom.

Identify the given information. The radius of the inner most orbit (n=1), also known as the Bohr radius, is \(r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}\). We need to find the radius of the third allowed orbit, so \(n = 3\).
Substitute \(n=3\) into the formula.
Calculate the value of \(r_3\) in meters.
Convert the result to Angstroms (Å) to match the options. Recall that \(1 \text{ Å} = 10^{-10} \text{ m}\).

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: According to the Bohr model, the radius of the nth orbit is proportional to \(n^2\), so \(r_n = r_1 n^2\). Given the radius of the first orbit (n=1) is \(r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}\), the radius of the third orbit (n=3) is \(r_3 = r_1 \times 3^2 = (5.3 \times 10^{-11}) \times 9 = 47.7 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}\). Since \(1 \text{Å} = 10^{-10} \text{m}\), this is equal to \(4.77 \text{Å}\).

Errors in unit conversion between meters and Angstroms.

question_text: A bullet from a gun is fired on a rectangular wooden block with velocity \(u\). When the bullet travels 24 cm through the block along its length horizontally, the velocity of the bullet becomes \(u/3\). Then it further penetrates into the block in the same direction before coming to rest exactly at the other end of the block. The total length of the block is:

explanation.summary: This problem involves motion with constant deceleration. We can use the equations of motion to analyze the bullet's movement in two parts. First, we find the deceleration from the first part of the journey. Then, we use this deceleration to find the additional distance the bullet travels before stopping.

step_by_step.description: Analyze the first part of the motion. The bullet travels a distance \(s_1 = 24 \text{ cm}\). The initial velocity is \(v_i = u\) and the final velocity is \(v_f = u/3\). Assume constant deceleration \(a\).
Apply the third equation of motion to find the deceleration \(a\).
Substitute the values for the first part of the motion.
Solve for the deceleration \(a\) in terms of \(u\).

Analyze the second part of the motion. The bullet travels an additional distance \(s_2\) until it comes to rest. The initial velocity for this part is \(v_i' = u/3\) and the final velocity is \(v_f' = 0\). The deceleration is the same, \(a = -u^2/54\).
Apply the third equation of motion again for the second part.
Substitute the values and solve for \(s_2\).
Simplify to find \(s_2\).
Calculate the total length of the block by adding the two distances.
step_by_step.formula: \text{Total Length} = s_1 + s_2 = 24 \text{ cm} + 3 \text{ cm} = 27 \text{ cm}

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: For the first 24 cm, using \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), we have \((u/3)^2 = u^2 + 2a(24)\), which gives \(2a = -8u^2 / (9 \times 24)\). For the remaining distance \(x\), the initial velocity is \(u/3\) and final is 0. So, \(0^2 = (u/3)^2 + 2ax\). Substituting \(2a\), we get \(x = -(u/3)^2 / (2a) = -(u^2/9) / (-8u^2 / (9 \times 24)) = 24/8 = 3 \text{ cm}\). The total length is \(24 \text{ cm} + 3 \text{ cm} = 27 \text{ cm}\).

Calculate the power (\(1/f_2\)) of the second lens.
Calculate the power (\(1/f_3\)) of the third lens.

Substitute the calculated powers.
Find a common denominator and solve.
Find the equivalent focal length \(F_{eq}\).

explanation.correct_option_reasoning: The system can be treated as three thin lenses in contact. The first and third lenses are plano-convex made of material with μ=1.5. The total power is \(P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 = 1/40 - 3/50 + 1/40 = 1/20 - 3/50 = (5-6)/100 = -1/100\). The equivalent focal length is \(F = 1/P = -100\) cm.
